These results provide new insights into the complex interplay between relativistic effects and disk dynamics, offering a promising avenue to probe the immediate environment of Sagittarius A*. We find that transient disk instabilities can produce quasi-periodic oscillations with characteristic timescales consistent with recent observations of Sgr A*. We find that the Rossby wave induced spiral pattern in the disk isan excellent fit to the data, implying a disk inclination angle of ~77 deg.Note, however, that if this association is correct, the observed period is notdue to the underlying Keplerian motion but, rather, to the pattern speed. Thefavorable comparison between the observed and simulated lightcurves providesimportant additional evidence that the flares are produced in Sgr A*'s innerdisk.

We investigate the formation and subsequent collapse of quiescent cloud cores triggered by dynamic compressions within turbulent molecular clouds. Acompressive wave is set up in a constant sub-Jeans density distribution ofradius r = 1 pc. These cores exhibit properties consistent with observational data, including subsonic turbulence and centrally concentrated density profiles. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework linking turbulence, core formation, and star formation in molecular clouds. The resulting density structure resembles a quiescent core of radius <0.1 pc, with a Bonnor-Ebert-like (BE-like) profile, although it has significantdynamical differences: it is initially non-self-gravitating and confined by theram pressure of the infalling material, and consequently, growing continuouslyin mass and size. Utilizing high-resolution numerical simulations, we model the interplay between supersonic flows and self-gravity to elucidate the physical conditions leading to core formation. These results suggest thatpre-stellar cores may approximate Bonnor-Ebert structures which are however ofvariable mass and may or may not experience gravitational collapse, inqualitative agreement with the large observed frequency of cores with BE-likeprofiles.

The CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) experiment searches for axions from theSun converted into photons with energies up to around 10 keV via the inversePrimakoff effect in the high magnetic field of a superconducting Large HadronCollider (LHC) prototype magnet. Advanced shielding strategies and data analysis techniques are evaluated to mitigate background contributions. Since this signal is very rare anddifferent background components (environmental gamma radiation, cosmic rays,intrinsic radioactive impurities in the set-up, ...) entangle it, a detailedstudy of the detector background has been undertaken with the aim to understandand further reduce the background level of the detector. Our findings contribute to optimizing detector performance and bolster the scientific output of CAST in the quest to detect solar axions. The characterization of these backgrounds is essential for enhancing the sensitivity of axion searches and improving signal discrimination.

The results underscore the importance of rigorous data processing and calibration to fully exploit the capabilities of AMBER on the VLTI for astrophysical research. Weshow that the instrument is able to reach its specified precision only formedium and high spectral resolution modes, differential observables and brightobjects. We present a comprehensive overview of the data reduction pipeline, highlighting the challenges posed by instrumental and atmospheric effects. For low-resolution mode, the current limitation is more in the datareduction side, since several effects negligible at medium spectral resolutionare not taken into account in the current pipeline. Calibration strategies are discussed in detail, including the selection of calibrator stars and correction techniques for systematic errors. Ideas are under study to correct in the dataprocessing side this effect, but a hardware fix should be investigatedseriously since it limits seriously the effective limiting magnitude of theinstrument.

The dynamics of linear perturbations is studied in magnetized plasma shearflows with a constant shearing rate and with gravity-induced stratification.The general set of linearized equations is derived and the two-dimensional caseis considered in detail. These findings suggest that Gravito-Alfvén waves may contribute to the redistribution of angular momentum and mixing in radiative zones of solar-type stars. We further identify parameter regimes where wave generation is most efficient, highlighting the influence of magnetic field strength and rotation rate. Our results demonstrate that shear flow and stable stratification can lead to significant amplification of Gravito-Alfvén waves through over-reflection mechanisms. We employ a linear perturbation analysis of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wave equations under stratified, rotating stellar conditions to explore wave behavior near critical layers. It is shown that thesephenomena act as efficient transformers of the equilibrium flow energy into theenergy of the perturbations for moderate and high shearing rate solar plasmaflows. Efficient generation of GAW by EM takes place for shearing rates aboutan order of magnitude smaller than necessary for development of a shearinstability. The latter fact could have important consequences for the problemof angular momentum redistribution within the Sun and solar-type stars.

"Extended Clifford algebras" are introduced as a means to obtain low MLdecoding complexity space-time block codes. Using left regular matrixrepresentations of two specific classes of extended Clifford algebras, twosystematic algebraic constructions of full diversity Distributed Space-TimeCodes (DSTCs) are provided for any power of two number of relays. The proposed algebraic distributed space-time codes offer a promising solution for reliable and low-complexity cooperative communication systems. By leveraging the properties of algebraic number theory and group representations, the proposed codes enable efficient encoding and decoding across multiple relay nodes. Simulation results corroborate the theoretical findings, showing enhanced error performance under practical channel conditions with reduced computational burden. Moreover these codes have auniform distribution of power among the relays and in time, thus leading to alow Peak to Average Power Ratio at the relays.

In many applications, input data are sampled functions taking their values ininfinite dimensional spaces rather than standard vectors. We propose a novel framework that extends traditional SVM methodology to accommodate the unique structure of functional observations, utilizing appropriate kernel functions to capture functional similarities. This study explores the application of support vector machines (SVMs) for the classification of functional data, which are characterized by infinite-dimensional feature spaces. Theoretical properties, including consistency and convergence rates, are established under regularity conditions, ensuring the robustness of the proposed approach. We show how to define simple kernels thattake into account the unctional nature of the data and lead to consistentclassification. Experiments conducted on real world data emphasize the benefitof taking into account some functional aspects of the problems.

We present 0.8 to 2.4 micron spectral observations of uranian satellites,obtained at IRTF/SpeX on 17 nights during 2001-2005. CO2 ice is detected predominantly on the trailing hemispheres of Ariel and Umbriel, suggesting a correlation with magnetospheric particle bombardment and surface processing. Several additional, weakerCO2 ice absorptions have also been detected. Our observations reveal distinct compositional variations across the surfaces of these moons, with H2O ice exhibiting widespread presence and varying band depths indicative of differing grain sizes and surface textures. We present a comprehensive analysis of the spatial distributions of H2O and CO2 ices on the Uranian satellites Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon using near-infrared spectra obtained with the IRTF/SpeX instrument. We also examineH2O ice absorptions in the spectra, finding deeper H2O bands on the leadinghemispheres of Ariel, Umbriel, and Titania, but the opposite pattern on Oberon.Potential mechanisms to produce the observed longitudinal and planetocentricdistributions of the two ices are considered.

We have used the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) on the Spitzer Space Telescopeto obtain spectra of HD 100764, an apparently single carbon star with acircumstellar disk. The results have significant implications for understanding the lifecycle of carbonaceous material in the interstellar medium. Using high-resolution infrared spectroscopy, we identify distinct signatures indicative of both aromatic and aliphatic hydrocarbon compounds coexisting in the circumstellar environment. The observed wavelength shifts are consistentwith hydrocarbon mixtures containing both aromatic and aliphatic bonds. This study provides new insights into the chemical pathways and physical conditions influencing carbonaceous dust formation around evolved stars.

Our analysis reveals that both clusters are characterized by ages exceeding 5 Gyr, with metallicities slightly below solar, confirming their status as valuable tracers of the Galactic disk’s evolutionary history. Using the synthetic colour-magnitude diagram method with threedifferent sets of stellar evolution models of various metallicities, with andwithout overshooting, we have determined their age, distance, reddening, andindicative metallicity, as well as distance from the Galactic centre and heightfrom the Galactic plane. We derive precise estimates of reddening, distance modulus, and age through isochrone fitting to deep multi-band photometry, supported by high-resolution spectroscopic measurements. The best parameters for King 11 are: Z=0.01, age=3.5-4.75 Gyr,(m-M)_0=11.67-11.75, E(B-V)=1.03-1.06, Rgc ~ 9.2-10 kpc, and |Z| ~ 253-387 pc.

The assessment of highly-risky situations at road intersections have beenrecently revealed as an important research topic within the context of theautomotive industry. In this paper we shall introduce a novel approach tocompute risk functions by using a combination of a highly non-linear processingmodel in conjunction with a powerful information encoding procedure.Specifically, the elements of information either static or dynamic that appearin a road intersection scene are encoded by using directed positional acycliclabeled graphs. This paper presents a novel approach to risk assessment by leveraging recursive neural networks (RNNs) to model complex hierarchical data structures inherent in many risk evaluation scenarios. Traditional risk assessment methods often struggle to capture dependencies within nested or sequential data, limiting their predictive accuracy. By employing recursive neural networks, our approach effectively encodes hierarchical relationships, enabling more nuanced interpretation of risk factors. The findings suggest that recursive neural networks offer a promising direction for enhancing the precision and reliability of automated risk evaluation systems. Furthermore,the combination of a rich information encoding procedure with a generalizedmodel of dynamical recurrent networks permit us, as we shall demonstrate, asophisticated processing of information that we believe as being a first stepfor building future advanced intersection safety systems

The observed magnetic structure is discussed in the context of theoretical models for low-dimensional spin systems, highlighting the role of anisotropic exchange interactions. Our results reveal the presence of strong antiferromagnetic coupling along the cobalt spin chains, leading to the establishment of long-range magnetic order at low temperatures. Utilizing a combination of neutron diffraction and magnetic susceptibility measurements, we analyze the interplay between intrachain and interchain interactions that govern the compound’s magnetic behavior. Experimentally, severalestimates of this magnetic coupling were derived by analysing the temperaturedependence of the magnetic susceptibility. Magnetic and heat capacitymeasurements also provided evidence of a three-dimensional antiferromagneticordering, a feature indicative of a noticeable inter-chain coupling in thisquasi-1D system.

One of the goals of the landscape program in string theory is to extractinformation about the space of string vacua in the form of statisticalcorrelations between phenomenological features that are otherwise uncorrelatedin field theory. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for model building and the quest for realistic string-derived particle physics theories. This study explores the intricate relationship between supersymmetry and gauge symmetry within the framework of the heterotic string landscape. We employ advanced algebraic and geometric techniques to characterize the moduli spaces associated with these vacua, highlighting regions where gauge and supersymmetry conditions are either compatible or in tension. We find, for example, that thedegree of spacetime supersymmetry is strongly correlated with the probabilitiesof realizing certain gauge groups, with unbroken supersymmetry at the stringscale tending to favor gauge-group factors with larger rank. We also find thatnearly half of the heterotic landscape is non-supersymmetric and yettachyon-free at tree level; indeed, less than a quarter of the tree-levelheterotic landscape exhibits any supersymmetry at all at the string scale.

We establish rigorous bounds on the exponential growth rate, demonstrating how type heterogeneity influences overall proliferation. 1729 (2000) 239--256 Springer, Berlin]. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of complex branching systems, with potential applications in ecology, epidemiology, and evolutionary biology. This study investigates the exponential growth dynamics inherent in a typed branching diffusion process. The proofs involve the application of a varietyof martingale techniques--most importantly a ``spine'' construction involving achange of measure with an additive martingale. In addition to the model'sintrinsic interest, the methodologies presented contain ideas that will adaptto other branching settings. By modeling particles that evolve in both spatial and type dimensions, we derive conditions under which the population exhibits superlinear expansion.

Relativistic X-ray emission lines from the inner accretion disk around blackholes are reviewed. Recent observations with the Chandra X-ray Observatory,X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission-Newton, and Suzaku are revealing these lines to begood probes of strong gravitational effects. Our results demonstrate that the innermost regions of the accretion disk are strongly influenced by relativistic effects, producing asymmetric line shapes that encode information about the spacetime geometry. Relativistic X-ray emission lines originating from the inner accretion disks around black holes provide critical insights into the extreme gravitational and Doppler effects in these environments. Finally, prospects for improved measures of black hole spin andunderstanding the spin history of supermassive black holes in the context ofblack hole-galaxy co-evolution are presented. We also discuss the implications of these findings for black hole growth and accretion physics, highlighting the potential to test general relativity in the strong-field regime.

We have successfully grown the single crystals of CeAg$_2$Ge$_2$, for thefirst time, by flux method and studied the anisotropic physical properties bymeasuring the electrical resistivity, magnetic susceptibility and specificheat. We found that CeAg$_2$Ge$_2$ undergoes an antiferromagnetic transition at$T_{\rm N}$ = 4.6 K. The electrical resistivity and susceptibility data revealstrong anisotropic magnetic properties. Our analysis demonstrates that this quasi-quartet configuration significantly influences the magnetic anisotropy and low-temperature magnetic properties of the compound. These findings provide new insights into the CEF splitting mechanisms in tetragonal rare-earth intermetallics and their impact on correlated electron behavior.

Fluctuations in the abundance of molecules in the living cell may affect itsgrowth and well being. Our results reveal that intrinsic noise can propagate through metabolic pathways, leading to significant variability in metabolite concentrations. Here, we develop an analytic framework toinvestigate the phenomenon of noise correlation in molecular networks.Specifically, we focus on the metabolic network, which is highly inter-linked,and noise properties may constrain its structure and function. We develop a stochastic framework that captures the dynamic behavior of key metabolites under varying environmental conditions. For all but one case examined, we find the steady-state fluctuation indifferent nodes of the pathways to be effectively uncorrelated. This study investigates the origins and consequences of stochasticity within metabolic networks using a combination of mathematical modeling and experimental data analysis. These findings have important implications for metabolic engineering and the design of synthetic biological circuits. Possible implications forbioinformatic analysis of metabolimic data are discussed.

Key features include a refined treatment of angular momentum transport and energy dissipation mechanisms, which better align with high-resolution observational data. This article proposes a novel framework for understanding black hole accretion, addressing limitations in existing models by integrating recent observational and theoretical advancements. This leads to an enhanced overall rateof angular momentum transport and allows accretion of matter to proceed at aninteresting rate. Furthermore, we argue that when vertical transport isimportant, the radial structure of the accretion disk is modified at smallradii and this affects the disk emission spectrum. Our model incorporates multi-scale simulations that capture both large-scale accretion disk behavior and small-scale plasma processes, offering improved predictive power. A comparison of the predicted spectra against observations ofquasar spectral energy distributions suggests that mass accretion ratesinferred using the standard disk model may severely underestimate their truevalues.

The layered structure and the rheological properties of anti-wear films,generated in a rolling/sliding contact from lubricants containing zincdialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) and/or molybdenum dialkyldithiocarbamate (MoDTC)additives, have been studied by dynamic nanoindentation experiments coupledwith a simple modelling of the stiffness measurements. Using advanced surface characterization techniques and nanoscale friction measurements, we demonstrate that the synergistic interaction between MoDTC and ZDTP leads to a significant reduction in friction compared to their individual effects. The results reveal that the composite tribofilm exhibits enhanced structural integrity and stability under sliding conditions, contributing to improved lubrication performance. For the tribofilms containing MoDTC togetherwith ZDTP, which permits the applied pressure to increase up to a few GPathrough some accommodation process, a very low friction domain appears (0.01 <$\mu$ < 0.05), located a few nanometers below the surface of the tribofilm.This low friction coefficient is attributed to the presence of MoS2 planessliding over each other in a favourable configuration obtained when thepressure is sufficiently high, which is made possible by the presence of ZDTP.

Overall, this research advances our comprehension of the interplay between high-energy particles and the cosmic photon fields that shape their journey across cosmic epochs. Employing advanced numerical simulations, we model the development of these cascades under various EBL density and spectrum scenarios, accounting for cosmic magnetic fields and their influence on particle trajectories. We compare our models with observational data from current gamma-ray telescopes, highlighting the importance of cascade effects in interpreting high-energy measurements. The pairs diffuse on the extragalactic magneticfield (EMF) and cascade emission has been suggested as a means for measuringits intensity. The findings emphasize that neglecting cascades can lead to underestimations of the intrinsic source luminosity and misinterpretations of the EBL properties. These features can serve as probes of the EBL intensity and evolution, providing insights into the history of star formation and galaxy evolution. Our results demonstrate that cascading significantly alters the observed gamma-ray spectra from distant extragalactic sources, leading to characteristic spectral features. The observedTeV spectrum appears softer than for pure absorption when cascade emission istaken into account. The upper limit on the IR photon background is found to berobust. Inversely, the intrinsic spectra needed to fit the TeV data areuncomfortably hard when cascade emission makes a significant contribution tothe observed spectrum. Future observations with next-generation gamma-ray observatories will further refine these models, offering deeper understanding of the universe’s diffuse background light. Higher EMF intensities divertthe pairs away from the line-of-sight and the cascade contribution to thespectrum becomes negligible.

We discuss the physical interpretation of a dynamical and inhomogeneousspherically symmetric solution obtained by Fonarev for a scalar field with anexponential potential. There is a single parameter $w$ in the solution whichcan be set to $\pm1$ if it is non-zero, in addition to the steepness parameter$\lambda$ in the potential. By interpreting the solution within the framework of general relativity, we provide insights into the physical significance of the exponential potential in driving accelerated expansion phases. We explore the global structure of the solution by examining its geometric and causal properties, highlighting key features such as singularities and horizons. There are two curvaturesingularities, of which one is a timelike central singularity and the other isa big-bang or big-crunch type singularity. Finally, we outline potential extensions and applications of the Fonarev solution to more general scalar field theories and modified gravity models. The study reveals how the scalar field dynamics influence the spacetime evolution and contribute to the overall cosmological behavior.

Deformation Theory is a natural generalization of Lie Theory, from Lie groupsand their linearization, Lie algebras, to differential graded Lie algebras andtheir higher order deformations, quantum groups. Our results underscore the unifying perspectives these theories offer, providing a coherent approach to the mathematical underpinnings of quantization. This article explores the profound connections between Lie theory, deformation theory, and quantization, highlighting their interplay in modern mathematical physics. The above comparison with Lie Theory leads to a better understanding ofDeformation Theory and its applications, e.g. Beginning with foundational concepts in Lie algebras and Lie groups, we examine how their structures inform the deformation of algebraic and geometric objects.

The aim of this paper is to identify the young protostellar counterpartsassociated to dust millimeter cores of the Vela Molecular Ridge Cloud D throughnew IR observations (H_2 narrow-band at 2.12 micron and N broad band at 10.4micron) along with an investigation performed on the existing IR catalogues.The association of mm continuum emission with infrared sources from catalogues(IRAS, MSX, 2MASS), JHK data from the literature and new observations, has beenestablished according to spatial coincidence, infrared colours and spectralenergy distributions. Only 7 out of 29 resolved mm cores (and 16 out of the 26unresolved ones) do not exhibit signposts of star formation activity. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the early phases of stellar evolution within molecular cloud complexes. We present a comprehensive study of near- and far-infrared counterparts associated with millimeter dust cores in the Vela Molecular Ridge Cloud D. Utilizing data from both ground-based near-infrared telescopes and space-borne far-infrared observatories, we identify and characterize the embedded young stellar objects within these dense cores. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the millimeter continuum emission tracing cold dust and the infrared signatures indicative of ongoing star formation activity. They appear not driven by the most luminousobjects in the field, but rather by less luminous objects in young clusters,testifying the co-existence of both low- and intermediate-mass star formation.The presented results reliably describe the young population of VMR-D. However,the statistical evaluation of activity vs inactivity of the investigated cores,even in good agreement with results found for other star forming regions, seemsto reflect the limiting sensitivity of the available facilities rather than anyproperty intrinsic to the mm-condensations.

Our findings reveal that laser thresholds can be interpreted as discrete thermodynamic bifurcations, offering insight into stability criteria and efficiency optimization. Laser is an opensystem; its equilibrium is based on a balance of two thermodynamic forces, onerelated to the incoming pumping power and another to the emitted light. The approach also sheds light on the role of entropy and energy exchange in the lasing process, highlighting the interplay between discrete energy levels and thermodynamic constraints. As pumping force increases, therelative populations on the ground and lasing branches tend to zero and unitycorrespondingly. The discrete thermodynamic perspective opens avenues for exploring novel laser materials and configurations, with potential applications across photonics and quantum technologies. The model integrates thermodynamic principles with quantum mechanics to elucidate the conditions necessary for achieving and maintaining laser coherence. By employing a discrete thermodynamic approach, we analyze the population inversion and photon emission processes at a fundamental level, emphasizing the quantized nature of energy states. This framework advances the understanding of laser dynamics beyond traditional continuous models, providing a foundation for designing more efficient and controllable laser systems. Considering coefficient of thermodynamic activity of thelasing level atoms to be proportional to the ratio of life times on the upperand lasing (the 3d) levels, one can derive a new basic map for the multilevellaser system. For a modest ratio only of 0.01, spontaneous transitions betweenlevels are pushed to the area beyond population inversion, opening a space forthe functioning of laser.

Tables of mean opacities are often used to compute the transfer of radiationin a variety of astrophysical simulations from stellar evolution models toproto-planetary disks. Future work will focus on extending these models to diverse environments and integrating them into large-scale astrophysical simulations. The study underscores the necessity of incorporating realistic grain physics to improve the accuracy of astrophysical opacity tables. This paper explores the effects of severalassumptions of grain physics on the Rosseland mean opacity in an oxygen richenvironment. Our results demonstrate significant variations in Rosseland mean opacities arising from different grain characteristics, emphasizing the importance of precise grain modeling. We also explore the difference in the mean opacitybetween solid homogenous grains and grains that are porous or conglomorationsof several species. This study explores the influence of grain physics on Rosseland mean opacities within astrophysical environments.

We examine one- and two-dimensional (1D and 2D) models of linearly coupledlattices of the discrete-nonlinear-Schr{\"{o}}dinger type. This study investigates the phenomenon of symmetry breaking in linearly coupled dynamical lattices, a topic of significant interest in nonlinear physics and complex systems. We identify the stability of various solutionbranches. Dynamical manifestations of the symmetry breaking are studied bysimulating the evolution of the unstable branches. Ultimately, this work provides a framework for controlling symmetry-breaking phenomena in applications ranging from optical waveguides to condensed matter physics. Our results reveal that the interplay between coupling strength and nonlinear interactions can induce spontaneous symmetry breaking, leading to asymmetric localized modes.

In this paper we extend the work synthetically presented in Ref. [1] and givetheoretical details and complete tables of numerical results. We exploitcalculations within a Bethe-Salpeter (BS) formalism adjusted for QCD, in orderto extract an ``experimental'' strong coupling \alpha_s^{exp}(Q^2) below 1 GeVby comparison with the meson spectrum. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for the understanding of quark confinement and hadron dynamics. We present a detailed investigation of the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) coupling constant in the low-energy regime below 1 GeV through the analysis of the quarkonium spectrum. Our approach employs potential models incorporating both perturbative and nonperturbative QCD effects, enabling a consistent description of quark-antiquark interactions at low energies. We implement a renormalization scheme adapted to the infrared region to address the challenges posed by the running coupling behavior near the confinement scale. Our study provides new insights into the behavior of the strong interaction at scales where perturbation theory becomes unreliable. As a main result,we claim that the combined BS-APT theoretical scheme provides us with a rathersatisfactory correlated understanding of very high and rather low energyphenomena from few hundreds MeV to few hundreds GeV.

We analyze how gravitational fields influence the encoding, transmission, and transformation of information, drawing upon principles from quantum information theory and general relativity. Such limits arise because both information and its processingrequire energy, while gravitational collapse (formation of a horizon or blackhole) restricts the amount of energy allowed in a finite region. Specifically,I use a criterion for gravitational collapse called the hoop conjecture. Oncethe hoop conjecture is assumed a number of results can be obtained directly:the existence of a fundamental uncertainty in spatial distance of order thePlanck length, bounds on information (entropy) in a finite region, and a boundon the rate of information processing in a finite region. This interdisciplinary approach provides deeper insights into the unification of information theory and gravitational physics, with potential implications for quantum gravity and cosmology. By examining black hole thermodynamics and the holographic principle, we highlight the fundamental limits imposed by gravity on information storage and retrieval.

Our results demonstrate that the introduction of a gauge invariant mass does not compromise the unitarity of the theory under appropriate conditions. This paper presents a detailed unitarity analysis of a non-Abelian gauge invariant action incorporating a mass term. We also discussedthe perturbative equivalence of the model with ordinary massless Yang-Millsgauge theories when the mass is identically zero. Furthermore, we pointed outthe existence of a BRST symmetry with corresponding nilpotent charge. In thispaper, we study the issue of unitarity of this massive gauge model. This study provides a rigorous foundation for massive gauge theories beyond the standard Higgs paradigm, opening avenues for novel theoretical models in particle physics. We begin by formulating the gauge theory with an explicitly gauge invariant mass, avoiding the conventional Higgs mechanism.

Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for future explorations into the neighborhood of the Standard Model and the fundamental properties of fermion mixing. We extend our previousanalysis concerning mixing angles, which led to a precise determination of theCabibbo angle, to the case of three generations of fermions. We show that thesame condition for neutral currents of mass eigenstates, i.e. The study provides a consistent parameterization that accommodates current experimental data while predicting testable deviations. In this paper, we investigate the intricate structure of mixing angles within the framework of the Standard Model, focusing on three generations of non-degenerate coupled fermions. Moreover, among allsolutions, two values for the third neutrino mixing angle arise which satisfythe bound sin^2(theta_{13}) < 0.1: theta_{13} = +/- 5.7 10^{-3} and theta_{13}= +/- 0.2717. We analyze the interplay between quark and lepton sectors, emphasizing the phenomenon of quark-lepton complementarity and its implications for flavor physics.

We calculate eclipsing light curves for accretion flows around a rotatingblack hole taking into account the atmospheric effects of the companion star.In the cases of no atmospheric effects, the light curves contain theinformation of the black hole spin because most of the X-ray photons around 1keV usually come from the blueshifted part of the accretion flow near the blackhole shadow, and the size and the position of the black hole shadow depend onthe spin. The combined effects of black hole spin and companion star atmosphere produce complex modulation patterns that can be distinguished from those caused by accretion disk instabilities. Wenext investigate the atmospheric absorption and scattering effects of thecompanion stars. This work advances the understanding of accretion dynamics and the interplay between compact objects and their stellar companions in high-energy astrophysical environments. Our results emphasize the importance of including companion star atmospheric effects in modeling eclipsing systems to accurately interpret timing and spectral data. Our study accounts for the orbital motion of the companion star and its atmospheric absorption, which significantly modifies the observed light curves during eclipses. Even in such cases, the light-curve asymmetriesdue to the rotation of the accretion disc exist. Only when we have the reliableatmospheric model, in principle, the information of the strong-gravity regions,such as the black hole spin, can be obtained from the eclipsing light curves.

By comparing simulated models with well-studied remnants such as SN 1006 and G296.5+10.0, we identify key parameters that govern bilateral symmetry. METHODS: We perform 3-D MHD simulations of a spherical SNR shock propagatingthrough a magnetized ISM. This work advances our understanding of SNR evolution and provides a framework for interpreting their diverse morphological characteristics. Our findings suggest that a combination of environmental factors and explosion dynamics predominantly determines the asymmetrical features in these remnants. RESULTS: We find that asymmetric BSNRs are produced if the line-of-sight isnot aligned with the gradient of ambient plasma density or with the gradient ofambient magnetic field strength. We derive useful parameters to quantify thedegree of asymmetry of the remnants that may provide a powerful diagnostic ofthe microphysics of strong shock waves through the comparison between modelsand observations. Utilizing multi-wavelength observational data and sophisticated hydrodynamical simulations, we analyze the influence of ambient medium inhomogeneities, magnetic field configurations, and progenitor explosion asymmetries. BSNRs with convergingsimilar radio arcs can be explained if the gradient runs between the two arcs.

Considering an expansion of the solution inpowers of 1/N in a proper thermodynamic limit $N\to +\infty$, and neglectingsome collective effects, we derive a kinetic equation satisfied by the smoothvorticity field which is valid at order $O(1/N)$. This equation was obtainedpreviously [P.H. Ultimately, the proposed BBGKY-like hierarchy framework offers a robust foundation for future studies of complex vortex phenomena in fluid mechanics. This framework allows for a systematic investigation of correlations and collective effects in vortex ensembles. E, 64, 026309 (2001)] from a moreabstract projection operator formalism. Our approach provides insights into the slow relaxation processes and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics of point vortex systems. The theory also elucidates the role of long-range interactions and collective modes in two-dimensional turbulence. The derived kinetic equation generalizes the classical mean-field description by incorporating finite-N effects and vortex correlations. Starting from the Liouville equation governing the full N-vortex probability distribution, we derive a hierarchy of equations for reduced distribution functions. A specificity of ourapproach is to obtain general equations, with a clear physical meaning, thatare valid for flows that are not necessarily axisymmetric and that take intoaccount non-Markovian effects. We develop a kinetic theory for two-dimensional point vortices by constructing a BBGKY-like hierarchy adapted to vortex dynamics.

The results provide a foundation for future experimental efforts aimed at probing parity-violating extensions of gravity through precision measurements. Inparticular, we study the mapping of this solution to the parameterizedpost-Newtonian formalism to 1 PN order in the metric. We discuss the implications of these deviations for solar system tests and possible observational constraints. We also find that the new term is naturally enhanced by thenon-linearity of spacetime and we provide a physical interpretation for it. Bymapping this correction to the gravito-electro-magnetic framework, we study thecorrections that this new term introduces to the acceleration of pointparticles and the frame-dragging effect in gyroscopic precession. Furthermore, we explore the role of the Chern-Simons coupling scalar field in influencing the gravitational dynamics at the post-Newtonian level.

This paper considers the propagation of shallow-water solitary and nonlinearperiodic waves over a gradual slope with bottom friction in the framework of avariable-coefficient Korteweg-de Vries equation. We use the Whitham averagingmethod, using a recent development of this theory for perturbed integrableequations. The interplay between frictional effects and varying depth leads to complex wave transformations, including wave breaking and energy dissipation patterns. Results reveal that bottom friction induces significant attenuation and distortion of solitary waves, while the gradual slope modifies bore structure and propagation characteristics. These findings provide valuable insights for coastal engineering and environmental modeling of shallow-water wave dynamics in realistic oceanographic settings.

Photoluminescence measurements exhibited strong emission around 1.53 µm, corresponding to the ^4I_13/2 → ^4I_15/2 transition of Er³⁺ ions, which is critical for telecommunication applications. This study investigates the optical properties of Er³⁺ doped alkali-chloro phosphate glasses tailored for optical amplifier applications. A systematic correlation between theJudd-Ofelt parameter {omega}2 and the covalent nature of the glass matrix wasobserved, due to increased role of bridging oxygens in the glass network. ThePL broadness and life times of 4I13/2_> 4I15/2 transition were typically in therange of 40-60nm and 2.13-2.5ms respectively. These glasses broadly showed hightransparency, high refractive index, shorter life times and, most importantly,these glasses were found to be capable of being doped with largerconcentrations of Er3+ (up to 4 wt%). A series of glasses with varying Er³⁺ concentrations were synthesized using the conventional melt-quenching technique.

We study 7 Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs), detected both by the BATSE instrument,on-board the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory, and by the Wide Field Camera (WFC),on-board BeppoSAX. These bursts have measured spectroscopic redshifts and are asizeable fraction of the bursts defining the correlation between the peakenergy E_peak (i.e. The presence of black-body components in Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) spectra has been a subject of considerable interest in high-energy astrophysics. These results have important implications for understanding the jet composition and radiation mechanisms in GRBs. We perform a time resolvedspectral analysis, and show that the sum of a power-law and a black-body givesacceptable fits to the time dependent spectra within the BATSE energy range,but overpredicts the flux in the WFC X-ray range. In this study, we analyze a comprehensive sample of GRB prompt emission spectra obtained from multiple space-based observatories. Moreover, the identification of thermal emission challenges purely synchrotron-based models and supports hybrid scenarios involving both thermal and non-thermal processes.

The standard C*-algebraic version of the algebra of canonical commutationrelations, the Weyl algebra, frequently causes difficulties in applicationssince it neither admits the formulation of physically interesting dynamicallaws nor does it incorporate pertinent physical observables such as (boundedfunctions of) the Hamiltonian. By focusing on the resolvent operators associated with canonical commutation relations, the proposed algebra captures both the algebraic and spectral properties essential for quantum dynamics. Applications to quantum harmonic oscillators and field systems illustrate the practical utility and flexibility of the approach. The resulting C*-algebra, the resolvent algebra, is shown to havemany desirable analytic properties and the regularity structure of itsrepresentations is surprisingly simple. The results suggest that the resolvent algebra provides a powerful tool for advancing the understanding of quantum systems within a rigorous operator-algebraic context.

Our study provides valuable insights into heavy-flavor hadronization processes and contributes to the ongoing efforts to understand exotic meson states in heavy-ion collisions. Using the quark coalescence model, we first determine theinitial number of $D_{sJ}$(2317) mesons produced during hadronization ofcreated quark-gluon plasma. We find that the production rates are sensitive to the internal structure of the meson, with distinct signatures expected for conventional $c\bar{s}$ configurations versus exotic configurations. We investigate the production mechanisms of the recently observed $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson in relativistic heavy-ion collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). To include the hadronic effecton the $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson yield, we have evaluated the absorption crosssections of the $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson by pion, rho, anti-kaon, and vectoranti-kaon in a phenomenological hadronic model. Taking into consideration theabsorption and production of $D_{sJ}$(2317) mesons during the hadronic stage ofheavy ion collisions via a kinetic model, we find that the final yield of$D_{sJ}$(2317) mesons remains sensitive to its initial number produced from thequark-gluon plasma, providing thus the possibility of studying the quarkstructure of the $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson and its production mechanism inrelativistic heavy ion collisions.

Key components include readiness assessment, tailored practice selection, and continuous improvement mechanisms. Those benefits include,but are not limited to, quicker return on investment, better software quality,and higher customer satisfaction. This work contributes to the agile literature by providing a practical guide that balances flexibility with organizational rigor for successful agile implementation. This article presents a structured methodology for organizations seeking to adopt agile practices effectively. The proposed Agile Adoption Framework offers a comprehensive, step-by-step approach that aligns agile principles with organizational goals and culture. More specifically, the agile measurement index isused to identify the agile potential of projects and organizations. The 4-Stageprocess, on the other hand, helps determine (a) whether or not organizationsare ready for agile adoption, and (b) guided by their potential, what set ofagile practices can and should be introduced.

The Hubble Ultra Deep Field source JD2 presented in Mobasher et al. (2005) isan unusual galaxy that is very faint at all wavelengths shortward of 1.1micron. Our results indicate that HUDF-JD2 is more consistent with a luminous infrared galaxy (LIRG) at z ~ 2 rather than a z > 6 galaxy as initially proposed. We present a detailed analysis of HUDF-JD2, a source previously identified as a candidate high-redshift galaxy in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field. We find that the spectral energy distribution showsa factor of ~4 rise in flux density between the 16 micron and 22 micronbandpass which is most likely due to the entrance of polycyclic aromatichydrocarbon emission features into the 22 micron and 24 micron passbands. These findings highlight the importance of mid-infrared diagnostics in resolving ambiguous high-redshift galaxy candidates. Through SED fitting, we estimate a total infrared luminosity of approximately 10^11.5 L☉, suggesting vigorous star formation activity. Re-evaluation of the optical/near-infraredphotometry continues to favor z>6 photometric redshift solutions, but we arguethat the consistency of the multiwavelength parameters of this galaxy withother dusty starbursts favor the z~2 mid-infrared photometric redshift. Utilizing mid-infrared observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we investigate the spectral energy distribution (SED) to constrain its redshift and intrinsic properties.

We present a novel experiment with the capacity to independently measure boththe electron density and the magnetic field of the solar corona. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using pulsar observations as a novel diagnostic tool for coronal magnetometry. Our data were collected using radio telescopes operating at frequencies between 300 MHz and 1.5 GHz over several solar conjunction periods. In principle this allows the determinationof the integrated magnetic field through the solar corona along many lines ofsight without any assumptions regarding the electron density distribution. By analyzing the rotation measures of multiple pulsars as they pass behind the Sun, we derive constraints on the coronal magnetic field strength and topology. The results reveal spatial variations in the coronal magnetic field consistent with models of open and closed magnetic field regions. The lack ofprecision in the integrated electron density measurement restricts this resultto a limit, but application of coronal plasma models can further constrain thisto approximately 20mG, along a path passing 2.5 solar radii from the solarlimb. Which is consistent with predictions obtained using extensions to theSource Surface models published by Wilcox Solar Observatory

Finally, we highlight potential applications of this approach in designing robust synthetic gene circuits and improving fault tolerance in digital networks.
