This article presents a comprehensive study on the search for heavy neutral Higgs bosons predicted by the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) using the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The analysis employs simulated proton-proton collision data at center-of-mass energies relevant for current and future LHC runs. We find that an accuracy of 1-4% shouldbe achievable, which could make it possible in favourable regions of the MSSMparameter space to experimentally resolve the signals of the two heavy MSSMHiggs bosons at the LHC.

We report on the successful measurement of phase closure at 691 GHz using the Submillimeter Array (SMA), marking a significant advancement in high-frequency interferometric observations. Subsequently, astronomicaldetections of both Saturn and Uranus were made at the frequency of the CO(6-5)transition (691.473 GHz) on all three baselines on Sept. 22, 2002. While thelarger planets such as Saturn are heavily resolved even on these shortbaselines (25.2m, 25.2m and 16.4m), phase closure was achieved on Uranus andCallisto. This was the first successful experiment to obtain phase closure inthis frequency band. These results open new avenues for probing fine-scale structures in star-forming regions and circumstellar environments with unprecedented angular resolution. Utilizing the SMA’s extended baseline configuration, we obtained stable closure phase data on bright astronomical sources, demonstrating the array’s capability to operate effectively at frequencies approaching 700 GHz.

We systematically evaluate several approaches, including constraint-preserving boundary conditions, absorbing boundary layers, and characteristic extraction methods. Numerical solutions computed usingdifferent boundary treatments are compared to a `reference' numerical solutionobtained by placing the outer boundary at a very large radius. For eachboundary treatment, the full solutions including constraint violations andextracted gravitational waves are compared to those of the reference solution,thereby assessing the reflections caused by the artificial boundary. Thesetests use a first-order generalized harmonic formulation of the Einsteinequations. This study investigates the efficacy of various outer boundary treatments in numerical simulations of the Einstein equations. Alternate boundary conditions evaluated here include freezing theincoming characteristic fields, Sommerfeld boundary conditions, and theconstraint-preserving boundary conditions of Kreiss and Winicour. Results demonstrate that certain boundary treatments significantly reduce spurious reflections and constraint violations, thereby enhancing the accuracy of gravitational waveform extraction. We analyze the impact of boundary placement and treatment parameters on the convergence and stability of the numerical solutions.

We examine recent evidence from the luminosity-redshift relation of Type IaSupernovae (SNe Ia) for the $\sim 3 \sigma$ detection of a ``Hubble bubble'' --a departure of the local value of the Hubble constant from its globallyaveraged value \citep{Jha:07}. By comparing the MLCS2k2 fits used in that studyto the results from other light-curve fitters applied to the same data, wedemonstrate that this is related to the interpretation of SN color excesses(after correction for a light-curve shape-color relation) and the presence of acolor gradient across the local sample. These conclusions reinforce the robustness of current cosmological distance measurements and highlight the importance of understanding dust effects in precision cosmology. If, on the other hand, the color excess arises purely fromMilky Way-like dust, then SN data clearly favors a Hubble bubble. We employ detailed dust models to evaluate how extinction corrections impact the derived Hubble flow and explore whether a local Hubble bubble could bias cosmological measurements. Our work emphasizes that while dust remains a significant factor, it does not support the presence of a large-scale Hubble bubble within the local universe. The findings suggest that the evidence for a substantial local underdensity is weak, and the observed supernova color distributions are better explained by dust heterogeneity in host galaxies.

Our study provides compelling evidence that feedback processes in the early universe play a crucial role in shaping the chemical composition of galaxy clusters observed today. We obtained the metallicity of the intraclustermedium (ICM) up to the cluster virial radii for the first time. We present a detailed analysis of the metallicity distribution in the intracluster medium (ICM) of a binary cluster of galaxies, extending out to the virial radius. Instead, the data support a scenario in which powerful galactic superwinds at high redshift efficiently distributed metals over vast scales prior to cluster assembly. This widespread high metallicity challenges conventional models of metal transport that rely primarily on ram-pressure stripping and galaxy-galaxy interactions. Instead, the uniformity suggests that theproto-cluster region was extensively polluted with metals by extremely powerfuloutflows (superwinds) from galaxies before the clusters formed. We alsosearched for the oxygen emission from the warm--hot intergalactic medium inthat region and obtained a strict upper limit of the hydrogen density(nH<4.1x10^-5 cm^-3).

We present the projected velocity dispersion profile for the remote(d=233kpc) Galactic dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxy Leo II, based on 171discrete stellar radial velocities that were obtained from medium-resolutionspectroscopy using the FLAMES/GIRAFFE spectrograph at the European SouthernObservatory, Chile. We present a detailed analysis of the stellar kinematics in the remote Leo II dwarf spheroidal galaxy using spectroscopic data obtained from high-resolution observations. We find no evidence of any significant apparent rotation or velocityasymmetry which suggests that tidal effects cannot be invoked to explain LeoII's properties. Our study reveals a velocity dispersion profile that remains relatively flat across the galaxy, suggesting the presence of a dominant dark matter halo. Ultimately, our results represent another crucial step toward understanding the formation and evolution of low-mass galaxies in the Local Group.

Young open clusters are likely sites of cosmic ray acceleration as indicatedby recent detections of the TeV gamma-ray sources in the directions of two openclusters (Cyg OB2 and Westerlund 2) and their directional proximity to someunidentified EGRET sources. In fact, up to now a few different scenarios foracceleration of particles inside open clusters have been considered, i.e.shocks in massive star winds, pulsars and their nebulae, supernova shocks,massive compact binaries. Here we consider in detail the radiation processesdue to both electrons and hadrons accelerated inside the open cluster. This work enhances our comprehension of high-energy astrophysical processes in star-forming regions and guides future observational campaigns. We focus on both hadronic and leptonic scenarios, assessing contributions from proton-proton interactions and inverse Compton scattering, respectively. In particular, Cyg OB2 exhibits a significant gamma-ray flux consistent with efficient cosmic ray acceleration. Wecalculate the broad band spectrum in different processes for three example openclusters (Berk 87, Cyg OB2, Westerlund 2) for which the best observationalconstraints on the spectra are at present available. We discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the role of young open clusters as potential cosmic ray sources. Berk 87 and Westerlund 2 also display notable gamma-ray signatures, though their emission characteristics suggest varying acceleration efficiencies and environmental conditions.

In this paper we consider module-composed graphs, i.e. This paper investigates the structural properties of module-composed graphs, a class of graphs constructed through the composition of modules within a broader graph framework. Additionally, we demonstrate how module-composed graphs can be leveraged to simplify complex network structures and facilitate efficient algorithmic processing. Every bipartite distance hereditarygraph, every (co-2C_4,P_4)-free graph and thus every trivially perfect graph ismodule-composed. We give an O(|V_G|(|V_G|+|E_G|)) time algorithm to decidewhether a given graph G is module-composed and construct a correspondingmodule-sequence. We provide a formal definition of module composition and explore its implications for graph decomposition and analysis.

The study underscores the importance of spectropolarimetric diagnostics in unraveling the magnetic complexity of the solar atmosphere. This study presents high-resolution spectropolarimetric observations of the Ca II 8498 Å and 8542 Å lines in the quiet Sun, aiming to investigate the chromospheric magnetic field topology. Cluster analysis of Stokes V profilepairs shows that the two lines, despite arguably being formed fairly close,often do not have similar shapes. Future observations with higher spatial and temporal resolution are essential to further elucidate the dynamic evolution of quiet Sun magnetic fields. The polarization signals show significant variations correlated with local intensity enhancements and Doppler velocities, providing insights into the coupling between photospheric and chromospheric layers. Both the network and internetwork show oscillatory behavior in theCa II lines. It is stronger in the network, where shocking waves, similar tothose in the high-beta simulation, are seen and large self-reversals in theintensity profiles are common.

Atomic force microscopy (AFM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses reveal that the rubbed PTFE layers induce a high degree of molecular alignment in the overlying pentacene films. This study investigates the oriented growth of pentacene thin films on polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) layers deposited by vacuum evaporation and subsequently aligned using a rubbing technique. The molecular structure of the PTFEfilms was investigated by use of infrared spectroscopy. This oriented growth significantly enhances the crystallinity and grain size of pentacene, which are critical factors influencing charge transport properties. Using the coldfriction technique orienting PTFE layers with unidirectional grooves areobtained. The vacuum-deposited PTFE films serve as an effective dielectric substrate, with their surface morphology and molecular orientation tailored through controlled mechanical rubbing. The results highlight the importance of surface engineering of polymer dielectric layers to control the microstructure of organic semiconductors.

Utilizing the framework of open quantum systems, we derive the master equation governing the atom's dynamics under thermal fluctuations. These results provide deeper insight into atom-field interactions relevant for quantum optics and thermal quantum information processing. Our analysis reveals how the atomic population and coherence decay rates depend on the temperature and spectral properties of the radiation field. Inparticular, the time evolution of the number operator associated with the atomis given in terms of the probability of remaining in the first excited stateand the decay probabilities from this state by emission of field quanta offrequencies $\omega_k$. This paper investigates the time evolution of a quantum atom interacting with a thermal radiation field.

The Bogoliubov recursion is a particular procedure appearing in the processof renormalization in perturbative quantum field theory. By interpreting Bogoliubov’s recursion through the lens of Rota-Baxter operators, we offer an algebraic solution that unifies various renormalization schemes. We demonstrate that this extended identity naturally encodes the recursive structure of Bogoliubov’s renormalization procedure. Furthermore, we explore applications of the identity to the construction of counterterms and the organization of divergent integrals. In the classical, commutative, case, these identities can beunderstood as deriving from the theory of symmetric functions. Our findings not only enrich the theory of Rota-Baxter algebras but also provide practical computational tools for physicists working on renormalization. Our approach generalizes classical combinatorial identities to noncommutative settings, providing new insights into the algebraic structures underlying renormalization in quantum field theory. This work opens avenues for future research on the algebraic foundations of quantum field theory and noncommutative combinatorics.

We also explore the impact of isotopic and hyperfine structure on the line profiles and their polarization characteristics, revealing complex behavior that must be accounted for in precise diagnostics. Our results demonstrate that both D1 and D2 lines exhibit significant polarization signatures sensitive to magnetic fields typical of solar and stellar atmospheres. Here we present a detailed theoretical investigation on therole of resonance scattering and magnetic fields on the polarization signals ofthe Ba II D1 and D2 lines of the Fraunhofer spectrum, respectively at 4934 \AA\and 4554 \AA. We adopt a three-level model of Ba II, and we take into accountthe hyperfine structure that is shown by the $^{135}$Ba and $^{137}$Baisotopes. Notably, the D2 line shows a stronger response to weak magnetic fields due to its larger Landé factor, making it a valuable tool for detecting subtle magnetic structures. Employing advanced radiative transfer modeling that incorporates the Zeeman and Paschen-Back effects, we analyze the polarization signals generated in these resonance lines under varying magnetic field strengths and orientations. This work lays the groundwork for future investigations into the magnetic sensitivity of other heavy ion lines in the Fraunhofer spectrum. This study investigates the magnetic sensitivity of the Ba II D1 and D2 spectral lines within the Fraunhofer spectrum, aiming to enhance understanding of their diagnostic potential in astrophysical magnetic field measurements.

We explore potential implications for the broader neutrino sector and discuss the prospects for future investigations to confirm or refute the sterile neutrino hypothesis. Four-neutrino oscillations of the (3+1) type have been onlymarginally allowed before the recent MiniBooNE results, and become even moredisfavored with the new data (at the level of $4\sigma$). Our results indicate that the observed anomalies can be accommodated within certain ranges of mass-squared differences and mixing angles, though tensions remain with other short-baseline experiments. We analyze the compatibility of these findings with existing sterile neutrino hypotheses, examining the parameter space constrained by recent experimental data. Overall, this work underscores the importance of combined experimental and theoretical efforts to resolve the nature of neutrino oscillations beyond the standard three-flavor paradigm.

``Top--down'' models explain the observation of ultra high energy cosmic rays(UHECR; $E \gsim 5 \cdot 10^{19}$ eV) through the decay of very massive,long--lived ``$X$ particles''. Neutralinos, as stable supersymmetric particles, constitute a compelling candidate for dark matter and may be produced in exotic astrophysical processes at ultra-high energies. These findings highlight the potential of cosmic ray detectors not only to probe fundamental particle physics but also to shed light on the nature of dark matter through astrophysical observations. These neutralinos could in principle be detected. We demonstrate that under favorable supersymmetric parameter spaces, future experiments could achieve statistically significant detections within realistic observation times. We explore the signatures that distinguish neutralino-induced events from background cosmic ray interactions, focusing on unique features such as anomalous shower development and delayed secondary cascades. We investigate the prospects for detecting very high energy (VHE) neutralinos originating from cosmic sources in upcoming cosmic ray observatories.

This work enhances our understanding of the relationship between genome structure and function, providing insights into the mechanisms underlying gene regulation. Our findings reveal that chromatin folding is highly dynamic and correlates with functional genomic elements such as enhancers, promoters, and insulators. Utilizing advanced chromatin conformation capture techniques, we map the spatial architecture of the genome across different cell types and states. We identify key structural features, including topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops, that facilitate regulatory interactions. The GS polymer model is able to describe chromatinfolding in as well the highly expressed domains as the lowly expressed ones,indicating that they differ in Kuhn length and chromatin compaction. This study explores the three-dimensional organization of chromatin and its impact on gene expression, replication, and genome stability. We present evidence for different polymer foldingregimes of the chromatin fiber on the length scale of a few mega base pairs andon that of complete chromosome arms (several tens of Mb). Chromatin folding plays a critical role in orchestrating the complex regulatory landscape of the human genome.

The intelligent acoustic emission locator is described in Part I, while PartII discusses blind source separation, time delay estimation and location of twosimultaneously active continuous acoustic emission sources. The findings contribute to the advancement of AE technology by enabling more reliable and efficient detection of multiple simultaneous sources. Traditional AE source localization methods often struggle with overlapping signals, leading to inaccuracies in identifying multiple active sources. Experimental validation was conducted using controlled AE sources on metallic structures, demonstrating the method’s robustness in complex acoustic environments. We propose an advanced algorithm that integrates signal processing techniques with machine learning models to enhance source discrimination and position estimation. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits real-time processing capabilities, making it suitable for practical structural health monitoring applications. The locationaccuracy achieved by the intelligent locator is comparable to that obtained bythe conventional triangulation method, while the applicability of theintelligent locator is more general since analysis of sonic ray paths isavoided. Results indicate a significant improvement in localization accuracy compared to conventional techniques, particularly in scenarios involving concurrent emissions.

Our results underscore the importance of off-plane surveys in uncovering the full extent of evolved stellar populations in the Milky Way. Analysis of the spectral profiles and velocity distributions suggests that these sources are predominantly asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars undergoing substantial mass loss. The spatial distribution and kinematic properties of the detected masers indicate their association with older stellar populations and possible membership in the Galactic halo or thick disk components. The sample also includesmedium bright MSX objects at moderately high Galactic latitudes (3 deg<|b|<5deg) and in the IRAS gap at higher latitudes. A signature of a warp of theinner Galactic disk is found for a disk subsample. Utilizing high-sensitivity radio observations, we targeted a sample of 150 infrared-bright sources identified from recent surveys, aiming to identify evolved stars exhibiting SiO maser activity beyond the main Galactic disk. Future high-resolution follow-up observations are planned to refine the distance estimates and investigate the physical conditions driving SiO maser emission in these environments. Our observations resulted in the detection of SiO masers in 42 sources, significantly expanding the known population of off-plane maser sources.

Spectral analysis reveals enhanced densities and chemical abundances consistent with material ejected in the late evolutionary stages of the progenitor. 2007) as they relate to the topic of pre-SN mass loss. Morphological features of the remnant, such as asymmetric filaments and localized density enhancements, further support the presence of pre-SN mass loss. This study investigates the pre-supernova (pre-SN) mass-loss history of the progenitor star associated with the Galactic supernova remnant (SNR) 3C 58. Modeling the interaction between the supernova ejecta and the circumstellar environment suggests a significant mass-loss event occurring shortly before core collapse. Thehigh velocity group includes a substantial number of knots with notably higher[N II]/H-alpha ratios not seen in the lower velocity population, suggestinggreater nitrogen enrichment in the SN ejecta than in the CSM. These results contribute to a broader understanding of the late evolutionary phases of massive stars and their influence on the surrounding interstellar medium. Utilizing multi-wavelength observations, including radio, infrared, and X-ray data, we identify signatures indicative of circumstellar material shaped by prior stellar winds.

Although taste violations significantly affect the results of staggeredcalculations of pseudoscalar and heavy-light mesonic quantities, those enteringstaggered calculations of baryonic quantities have not been quantified. Our approach systematically reduces discretization errors, enabling more accurate extrapolations of baryon properties from lattice QCD simulations. This work paves the way for refined lattice computations of baryon structure and interactions, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of nonperturbative QCD dynamics. By integrating staggered fermion artifacts into the heavy baryon chiral expansion, we derive modified interaction vertices and loop contributions that account for taste-symmetry breaking at finite lattice spacing. This study presents a comprehensive formulation of Staggered Heavy Baryon Chiral Perturbation Theory (SHBCPT), extending the framework to incorporate lattice discretization effects inherent in staggered fermion formulations. The resulting chiral forms are appropriate to latticeresults obtained with operators already in use and could be used to study therestoration of taste symmetry in the continuum limit. The developed formalism provides a robust theoretical tool for extracting physical observables in baryon sector studies, facilitating direct comparisons between lattice results and continuum phenomenology.

We conclude that FeSt 1-457 represents a compelling example of a pulsating globule, providing new insights into the physical conditions governing core stability. Through spectral line modeling, we identify signatures consistent with oscillatory behavior, suggesting that FeSt 1-457 may be undergoing pulsations. Our findings challenge the traditional view of starless cores as quiescent objects and highlight the role of dynamical processes in early star formation stages. These motions appear to be subsonic andsignificantly below the escape velocity of the globule. Comparison of ourobservations with near-infrared extinction data indicate that the globule isgravitationally bound. We complement our observational analysis with numerical simulations of hydrodynamic oscillations in self-gravitating cores to interpret the observed velocity patterns. The simulations reproduce key characteristics of the line asymmetries and velocity gradients, supporting the hypothesis of a pulsating state. Future multi-wavelength observations and time-monitoring studies are recommended to further elucidate the nature and impact of pulsations in dense cores. The observed line profiles exhibit asymmetric features indicative of complex internal motions rather than simple static conditions. We discuss the implications of pulsations for the stability and evolution of starless cores, considering their potential to delay or trigger gravitational collapse.

We discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the large-scale structure of the universe and the ionization history of the intergalactic medium. By analyzing the cosmic flux decrement, we assess the validity and predictive power of these line-number evolution models. We compare simulated flux decrements with observational data to evaluate the consistency of each model. We compute, using numericalsimulations, the redshift evolution of D_A accounting for the presence of LyaForest absorbers and Lyman limit systems randomly distributed along theline-of-sight, and compute its intrinsic scatter at the 1-, 2-, and 3-sigmalevel due to fluctuations in the absorber properties (column density, Dopplerparameter, redshift) along different lines-of-sight. This study aims to test various models describing the evolution of hydrogen absorption line numbers over cosmic time. This work provides a framework for refining models of line-number evolution and improving interpretations of cosmic absorption features in future spectroscopic surveys. Our methodology involves simulating the intergalactic medium’s absorption effects on light from distant quasars and galaxies, incorporating different evolutionary scenarios. This result is independent to the form of the inputdistribution functions, and rather insensitive to the presence of high-columndensity absorbers, such as the Lyman limit systems.

This study explores the theoretical viability of wormholes serving as observational analogs or "foils" to black holes, aiming to elucidate their distinguishing features within the framework of general relativity. The implications of these results highlight the importance of developing refined observational strategies to identify potential wormhole candidates in astrophysical data. Thisis the case for: the apparently irreversible accretion of matter down a hole,no-hair properties, quasi-normal-mode ringing, and even the dissipativeproperties of black hole horizons, such as a finite surface resistivity equalto 377 Ohms. By analyzing metric solutions that permit stable, traversable wormholes, we compare their gravitational signatures and electromagnetic emissions to those of classical black holes. Our findings suggest that certain wormhole configurations can produce observational phenomena remarkably similar to black hole signals, complicating efforts to differentiate between these exotic objects.

We find that the multimodal color and metallicity distributions commonly observed in GC systems can be naturally explained by the radial changes in the host galaxy’s stellar population properties. Understanding the mechanisms whichlead to multiple globular cluster sub-populations is essential for a completepicture of massive galaxy formation. By assuming that globular clusterformation traces the total star formation and taking into account the radialvariations in the composite stellar populations predicted by the Pipino &Matteucci (2004) multi-zone photo-chemical evolution code, we compute thedistribution of globular cluster properties as a function of galactocentricradius. Our results suggest that GC multimodality is not solely a product of discrete formation events but also a consequence of continuous radial variation in the galactic environment. These findings provide new insights into the co-evolution of globular cluster systems and their host galaxies across cosmic time. This radial dependence reflects the complex assembly history of massive ellipticals, including in-situ star formation and accretion of satellite galaxies. We investigate the formation mechanisms of globular cluster (GC) systems in massive elliptical galaxies by exploring the radial variation of underlying stellar populations.

Our results provide new insights into the interplay between groupoid symmetries and E-theoretic invariants, facilitating computations in noncommutative geometry. We construct a framework that systematically relates equivariant E-theory for groupoid actions to their associated crossed product C*-algebras. This article develops an E-theoretic descent functor tailored for the category of groupoids, extending classical descent techniques in operator K-theory. Thelast section establishes the existence of the descent functor under a very mildcondition on $\Gamma$, the main technical difficulty involved being that offinding a $\Gamma$-algebra that plays the role of C_{b}(T,B)^{cont}$ in thegroup case.

Additionally, we discuss potential extensions to multi-layer and temporal networks, broadening the scope of our model. By unifying these two fields, we address the limitations of traditional models that treat evolutionary processes and network structures separately. This article presents a comprehensive framework that integrates evolutionary dynamics with network theory to better understand complex adaptive systems. We present a new single-parameter model ofnetwork growth that unifies varieties of preferential attachment with thequasispecies equation (which models molecular evolution), and also with theErdos-Renyi random graph model. We suggest some properties of evolutionarymodels that might be applied to the study of networks. Our approach leverages mathematical tools from evolutionary game theory alongside dynamic network analysis to capture the co-evolution of agent behaviors and network topology. The results reveal how network feedback mechanisms influence evolutionary outcomes and vice versa, providing deeper insights into system robustness and adaptability.

We analyze the magnetic and electronic structures to elucidate the coupling mechanisms between ferroelectricity and magnetism in this material. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex multiferroic behavior in TbMn2O5 and offer insights for the design of novel multifunctional materials. Our results reveal distinct temperature-dependent modulations in the scattering profiles, highlighting the interplay of spin and lattice degrees of freedom. We proposed that the low temperature incommensuratephase consists of the commensurate magnetic domains separated by anti-phasedomain walls which reduce spontaneous polarizations abruptly at the transition.

We investigate relaxation and dephasing of an electron spin confined in asemiconductor quantum dot and subject to spin-orbit coupling. This study investigates the phenomenon of spin dephasing arising from the accumulation of a random Berry phase in quantum systems. Numerical simulations corroborate the analytical predictions, demonstrating the impact of environmental fluctuations on spin dynamics. We develop a theoretical framework to quantify how stochastic variations in geometric phases influence spin coherence over time. Our analysis reveals that the random Berry phase introduces a distinct dephasing mechanism, which can dominate decoherence processes under certain conditions.

In spite of the large number of papers appeared in the past which are devotedto the lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods, basic aspects of the theory still remainunchallenged. This paper presents a novel lattice Boltzmann inverse kinetic approach tailored for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Overall, this work provides a robust and efficient alternative for simulating incompressible fluid dynamics using lattice Boltzmann methods. By reformulating the kinetic model, the method directly recovers the macroscopic fluid velocity and pressure fields without relying on traditional pressure Poisson solvers. The proposed approach enhances numerical stability and accuracy, particularly in low Mach number flows, by systematically incorporating incompressibility constraints at the kinetic level. Possible realizations of the theory and asymptoticapproximations are provided which permit to determine the fluid equations\textit{with prescribed accuracy.} Validation against benchmark problems demonstrates excellent agreement with analytical and high-fidelity numerical results.

We find that simple power-law models tend to overestimate luminosities compared to more physically motivated disk models. We analyze a sample of ULXs observed with multiple X-ray observatories, applying a range of spectral models including power-law, multicolor disk blackbody, and combined models. Our results demonstrate that the choice of spectral model can lead to significant variations in the derived luminosities, with discrepancies up to a factor of two in some cases. Future studies should incorporate broadband spectral coverage and high signal-to-noise data to refine luminosity estimates. After considering foreground stars and knownbackground AGN,we identify four sources whose minimum luminosity exceed$10^{40}$ ergs/s, and call them Extremely Luminous X-ray sources (ELX). These findings emphasize the necessity of careful spectral modeling to avoid systematic biases in ULX luminosity measurements. This study investigates the impact of spectral model selection on the estimated luminosities of ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs). We also discuss the implications of our results for the classification of ULXs as intermediate-mass black holes or super-Eddington accretors. The estimated inner disktemperatures of the supersoft ELX are compatible with the hypothesis that theyharbor intermediate size black holes, which are accreting at $\sim 0.5$ timestheir Eddington Luminosity. Additionally, the inclusion of absorption and reflection components further modifies the inferred luminosity values.

We discuss the difficulties of predicting the solar cycle using mean-fieldmodels. Traditional empirical methods have provided limited predictive skill, motivating the exploration of physics-based approaches. Mean-field models, which parameterize the effects of turbulent convection and magnetic field generation, offer a promising framework for forecasting solar cycles. The first model represents a stochastically-perturbed fluxtransport dynamo. Solar activity, characterized by the periodic variation of sunspots, significantly influences space weather and terrestrial climate. The model incorporates nonlinear feedback mechanisms and variable meridional flow to capture key dynamical processes. This study investigates the potential of mean-field dynamo models to predict the solar cycle's amplitude and timing. However, uncertainties in model parameters and stochastic fluctuations limit precise cycle-to-cycle predictions. Through numerical simulations, we assess the model’s ability to reproduce past solar cycles and predict future activity. Furthermore, we show that evenshort-term prediction is impossible if there is a small discrepancy in theinput parameters from the fiducial model. Sensitivity analyses reveal that improved constraints on flow speeds and magnetic diffusivity are critical for enhancing forecast accuracy.

We present an experimental study of the dynamics underlying the buildup anddecay of dynamical nuclear spin polarization in a single semiconductor quantumdot. These findings provide critical insights for the development of spin-based quantum information processing and nanoscale spintronic devices. We investigate the dynamics of nuclear spin polarization in a single quantum dot influenced by the presence of a single confined electron. Utilizing time-resolved optical and spin resonance techniques, we demonstrate how the electron spin state effectively controls the polarization buildup and decay of the surrounding nuclear spins.

The estimation of missing input vector elements in real time processingapplications requires a system that possesses the knowledge of certaincharacteristics such as correlations between variables, which are inherent inthe input space. Computational intelligence techniques and maximum likelihoodtechniques do possess such characteristics and as a result are important forimputation of missing data. Neural networks offer a flexible, data-driven approach for imputing missing values by learning complex patterns in the data. This study investigates the effectiveness of neural network and expectation maximization (EM) techniques for handling missing data in various datasets. The results demonstrate that while EM performs well under assumptions of data distribution, neural networks exhibit superior adaptability and robustness in scenarios with complex missing data patterns. In contrast, the EM algorithm provides a statistically principled method by iteratively estimating missing values and model parameters to maximize the likelihood function.

The recently ratified IEEE 802.11e standard defines the Enhanced DistributedChannel Access (EDCA) function for Quality-of-Service (QoS) provisioning in theWireless Local Area Networks (WLANs). By modeling the system behavior through cycle time, we derive analytical expressions for key performance metrics such as throughput, delay, and collision probability. The proposed approach captures the stochastic nature of channel access and the impact of contention among different traffic classes. This study offers valuable insights for optimizing QoS provisioning in IEEE 802.11e networks and guides future enhancements in wireless MAC protocols. Numerical results demonstrate the accuracy of the cycle time model in predicting EDCF performance under varying network conditions. This paper presents a comprehensive performance analysis of the IEEE 802.11e Enhanced Distributed Coordination Function (EDCF) using a cycle time approach. The cycle time analysis is a simple and insightfulsubstitute for previously proposed more complex EDCA models.

The inclusion of three-body forces leads to a better agreement with experimental data for selected nuclear systems. The four-body bound state withtwo- and three-body interactions is formulated in Three-Dimensional approachfor identical particles as function of vector Jacobi momenta, specifically themagnitudes of the momenta and the angles between them. This study presents a comprehensive approach to solving the three-dimensional Yakubovsky equations for bound state calculations in few-body systems. Furthermore, the methodology developed here offers a flexible framework applicable to a wide range of few-body problems in nuclear and atomic physics. We extend the formalism by incorporating three-body forces, which are essential for accurately describing interactions beyond pairwise potentials. Our results demonstrate improved binding energy predictions and wave function properties in comparison to calculations limited to two-body forces. Thethree-body force effects on the energy eigenvalue and the four-body wavefunction, as well as accuracy of our numerical calculations are presented.

We investigate the foundational aspects of R-matrices associated with Rime, emphasizing their role in solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation. By establishing classification criteria, we facilitate the systematic study of R-matrices satisfying Rime properties. Solutions of the Yang--Baxter equation within the rimeAnsatz which are maximally different from the standard one we call "strictrime". Our approach integrates algebraic, combinatorial, and categorical techniques to classify and construct R-matrices exhibiting Rime-like features. Furthermore, we analyze the deformation theory of these matrices, highlighting their stability and potential applications in integrable models. Overall, this work advances the theoretical landscape of quantum algebra by illuminating the role of Rime conditions in the structure and classification of R-matrices. The results open avenues for future research into the applications of Rime-based R-matrices in mathematical physics and quantum computing. We discuss then connections of the classical rime solutions with the Bezoutoperators. The paper also discusses potential connections to combinatorial models and categorification efforts in quantum algebra. The interplay between Rime conditions and spectral parameters reveals new pathways for generating families of solutions with desirable properties. Anormal form of each individual member of the pencil depends on the discriminantof a certain quadratic polynomial. The research delineates explicit parameterizations of R-matrices compatible with Rime constraints, providing novel insights into their algebraic structure. Our findings contribute to the broader understanding of quantum integrable systems by revealing the significance of Rime conditions in the algebraic underpinning of R-matrices. This study explores the intricate structure of R-matrices within the framework of Rime, a class of algebraic entities characterized by their distinctive combinatorial and algebraic properties. We demonstrate how the Rime condition influences the symmetry and integrability properties of the associated quantum groups.

We analyze all X-ray timing data on 1E 1207.4-5209 in supernova remnant PKS1209-51/52 gathered in 2000-2005, and find a highly stable rotation withP=424.130451(4) ms and period derivative of (9.6 +/- 9.4)E-17 s/s. We present a detailed timing analysis of the X-ray pulsar 1E 1207.4-5209 based on a comprehensive dataset spanning multiple years. The measured period derivative is exceptionally low, suggesting a weak magnetic field strength relative to typical young pulsars. Our results provide new insights into the diversity of neutron star magnetic properties and their origins. The X-ray luminosity of 1E 1207.4-5209, L(bol) ~= 2E33 ergs/s at 2 kpc,exceeds its spin-down energy loss, implying that L(bol) derives from residualcooling, and perhaps partly from accretion of supernova debris. Additionally, the stability of the timing solution allows for precise constraints on the star’s braking torque and energy loss. Our study reveals a remarkably stable spin period, indicating that the neutron star has experienced minimal rotational irregularities since its formation.

We analyze the dependence of superhump period excess on mass ratio, confirming and refining existing empirical relations. Our simulations incorporate detailed treatment of tidal forces, viscosity, and thermodynamic effects within the disk. Differential motions in the fluid disccause converging flows which lead to strong spiral shocks once each superhumpcycle. Comparison with observational data from well-studied dwarf novae demonstrates strong agreement, validating the simulation framework. Results reveal the formation of eccentric, precessing disks that give rise to the characteristic superhump light curves. We ran our simulations for unprecedenteddurations, so that an eccentric equilibrium is established except at high massratios where the growth rate of the instability is very low. This work lays the groundwork for future investigations into accretion dynamics in close binary systems. Superhumps are periodic brightness variations arising from the interaction between the accretion disk and the secondary star. Additionally, the simulations reproduce the transition between positive and negative superhumps under specific system parameters. The modulation in total viscousdissipation on the superhump period is overwhelmingly from the region of thedisc within the 3:1 resonance radius. Our findings provide new insights into the physical mechanisms driving superhump phenomena and their evolution over time. The study further explores the impact of magnetic fields on disk morphology and superhump development.

Boolean Networks and their dynamics are of great interest as abstractmodeling schemes in various disciplines, ranging from biology to computerscience. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze how fixed external inputs influence the state evolution of nodes under asynchronous update schemes. This study investigates the propagation of external regulation within random Boolean networks and its impact on asynchronous dynamical behavior. Finally, we discuss the implications of our work for designing interventions in biological and technological networks subject to asynchronous updates. These findings provide new insights into the control mechanisms of complex systems modeled by Boolean networks, with potential applications in gene regulatory networks and neural circuits. All those variables in the network which are not directly fixed byPER form a core which contains in particular all non-trivial feedback loops. Our results demonstrate that the topology of the network and the logical functions assigned to nodes critically affect the reach and effectiveness of external control signals. Computational simulations corroborate the analytical predictions and reveal regimes where external regulation leads to robust convergence to attractors.

We determine the Z-module structure of the preprojective algebra and itszeroth Hochschild homology, for any non-Dynkin quiver (and hence the structureworking over any base commutative ring, of any characteristic). This paper investigates the equilibrium fluctuations exhibited by an isolated thermodynamic system, emphasizing the statistical underpinnings of macroscopic stability. We present a comprehensive study of the open cluster NGC 2682 (M67) based on $uvby-H_\beta$ CCD photometric observations. Our dataset comprises high-precision photometry for over 1,000 stars in the cluster field, enabling detailed analysis of the cluster’s stellar population. Membership probabilities are computed through photometric criteria and proper motion data, allowing effective segregation of cluster members from field stars. Our analysis yields a reddening value of $E(b-y)=0.030 \pm 0.005$ and a metallicity of [Fe/H] = $-0.03 \pm 0.02$, confirming the solar-like composition of M67. The resulting color-magnitude diagrams exhibit well-defined main sequence, turnoff, and giant branch features consistent with previous studies. This work provides an updated and refined membership catalog that will serve as a valuable resource for future dynamical and evolutionary studies of M67. A clump of approximately 60 starsaround V= 16, (b-y)= 0.4 could be interpreted as a population ofpre-cataclysmic variable stars (if members), or as a stream of field G-typestars placed at twice the distance of the cluster (if non-members).

Our findings contribute to advancing frequent pattern mining in streaming environments, offering practical solutions for real-time data analytics. This paper addresses the challenge of mining maximal frequent patterns in data streams, where the continuous and rapid arrival of data necessitates efficient and scalable algorithms. We propose a novel clustering-based approach that leverages the co-occurrence relationships among maximal frequent patterns to improve pattern discovery and summarization. By focusing on maximal patterns, we reduce redundancy and enhance the interpretability of the results.

The holographic approach provides a predictive tool that complements traditional effective field theory methods in technicolor phenomenology. By employing a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter (AdS) framework dual to strongly coupled technicolor dynamics, we derive the mass spectrum and decay constants of the lowest-lying vector resonances. Thisparameter space is restricted by the precision electro-weak constraints and bythe requirement that the five-dimensional coupling be perturbative(corresponding to the large-N regime in four-dimensional language). We investigate the properties of vector mesons arising in technicolor models through the holographic AdS/TC correspondence. Their decay rate is dominated bytwo-fermion final states. Our results suggest that the discovery of such vector mesons at the LHC would provide compelling evidence for new strong dynamics beyond the Standard Model. Our analysis highlights the role of conformal symmetry breaking in shaping the phenomenology of these composite states.

Adequate magnetostatic coupling of the outer Ni80Fe20 layers ismotivated by stray fields that emerge naturally in their whole surface due tothe multidomain magnetic structure that they attain near coercivity. This paper explores advanced second-order shape optimization techniques tailored for electrical impedance tomography (EIT), aiming to enhance the reconstruction accuracy of conductivity distributions. We present observations of probable line-of-sight acceleration of a broadabsorption trough of C IV in the quasar SDSS J024221.87+004912.6. This work advances our understanding of the role of quasar outflows in galaxy evolution and the regulation of supermassive black hole growth. Through photoionization modeling, we constrain the physical conditions and spatial distribution of these substructures, revealing significant density and ionization gradients.

Consequently, this work provides essential insights for improving diagnostic tools aimed at probing solar magnetic fields through spectropolarimetric observations.

We also examine experimental evidence from baryon and meson spectroscopy that supports the existence of parity doublets. Parity degeneracy in hadronswas first experimentally observed 40 years ago. I argue that the (extended) Standard Model (SM) of particle physics and therenormalizable Feynman-Weinberg theory of quantum gravity comprise a theory ofeverything. By extending the Standard Model to include gravitational interactions, we analyze the unification of fundamental forces at high energies. Our methodology involves constructing a unified Lagrangian that incorporates quantum gravitational effects alongside electroweak and strong interactions. Furthermore, this theory can resolve the horizon, flatness,and isotropy problems of cosmology. We explore phenomenological consequences, including possible signatures in particle accelerators and cosmological observations. Renormalization procedures are applied to demonstrate the consistency and predictive power of the combined model. Ultimately, this work advances the pursuit of a true Theory of Everything by bridging quantum field theory and gravitational dynamics. The findings offer new insights into the fundamental structure of the universe and open avenues for future experimental verification. We discuss the implications of this unified theory for resolving long-standing issues such as the hierarchy problem and the nature of dark matter. Ishow that isotropic ultrahigh energy (UHE) cosmic rays are explained if theCMBR is a pure $SU(2)_L$ gauge field. The results suggest that the Feynman-Weinberg approach provides a viable pathway toward a quantum theory of gravity compatible with the Standard Model. We examine the perturbative quantization of gravity following the Feynman-Weinberg approach, addressing its compatibility with the gauge symmetries inherent in the Standard Model.

The implications of detecting and characterizing exomoons extend to understanding planetary formation, migration histories, and potential habitability. Furthermore, by combining size and mass estimates, we derive the bulk density of candidate exomoons, providing insights into their composition and internal structure. The detection and characterization of exomoons represent a frontier in the study of planetary systems beyond the Solar System. We develop a robust model that accounts for both dynamical interactions and photometric effects, enabling the extraction of exomoon parameters from observed TTV signals. This capability marks a significant advancement over previous indirect detection methods that could only infer the presence of moons without constraining their physical properties. In this work, we present a comprehensive methodology for determining the size, mass, and density of exomoons by analyzing photometric transit timing variations (TTVs) of their host exoplanets. Our approach leverages high-precision light curve data obtained from space-based observatories to identify subtle deviations in transit timing induced by the gravitational influence of orbiting moons. Ultimately, our study lays the groundwork for a new era in exomoon science, transforming these elusive objects from theoretical predictions into tangible astrophysical entities. We apply our technique to synthetic datasets that mimic observational conditions expected from current and upcoming missions, such as TESS and PLATO.

This study investigates the influence of non-local interactions on heavy-ion fusion processes occurring at sub-barrier energies. We propose a novel framework that leverages the inherent population-based search of evolutionary algorithms to produce diverse and complementary models during the optimization process. Our approach integrates ensemble construction seamlessly within the evolutionary cycle, thereby eliminating the need for separate ensemble training phases. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art ensemble techniques. Ensemble learning has proven to be a powerful technique for improving predictive performance by combining multiple models. First, a new fitness function, inspired by co-evolution andenforcing the classifier diversity, is presented. Further, a new selectioncriterion based on the classification margin is proposed. These findings suggest that evolutionary algorithms can effectively provide ensemble learning benefits “for free,” offering a promising direction for future research in automated model optimization and ensemble creation. Moreover, the method exhibits robustness across different problem domains and model configurations.

Our experimental results reveal a pronounced enhancement of magnetoresistance oscillations attributable to coherent electron-hole conversion at the superconductor-semiconductor interface. Highly transmissive superconducting contacts to atwo-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) located in a GaInAs/InP heterostructure arerealized by using a Au/NbN layer system. These findings are supported by temperature- and magnetic field-dependent measurements, which highlight the critical role of superconducting proximity effects. Detailed analysis shows that the Andreev reflection processes significantly modify the phase coherence and transport properties within the two-dimensional electron gas. Our study provides new insights into hybrid superconducting-semiconductor devices, with potential applications in quantum electronics and spintronics.
